For the catalytically inactive S195A CTRC, no K  D  values were previously determined; therefore, we followed a different approach. In parallel with competitive FP titrations on the wt CTRC, we performed a series of competitive FP titrations on S195A CTRC as well, using the same FL-SGPI-2 I1 tracer and the 12 SGPI-2 variants. We already knew from direct titration that S195A CTRC and FL-SGPI-2 I1 interact with picomolar affinity, and from the competitive measurements, we saw that SGPI-2 I6 has a binding affinity to S195A CTRC that could be determined by direct titration. Therefore, we FITC labeled SGPI-2 I6 and determined its K  D  for S195A CTRC in a direct titration FP measurement (Figure S3a). Then, we performed competitive titration FP measurement using SGPI-2 I6, FL-SGPI-2 I6, and S195A CTRC and obtained the K  D  for the interaction between S195A CTRC and unlabelled SGPI-2 I6 (Figure S3b). This value was then used to determine the K  D  for the FL-SGPI-2 I1-S195A CTRC interaction in a competitive titration FP measurement using SGPI-2 I6, FL-SGPI-2 I1, and S195A CTRC (Figure S3c). Finally, we evaluated the series of competitive FP titrations on the inactive enzyme on all 12 SGPI-2 variants using FL-SGPI-2 I1 as tracer (Figure S5).

For the catalytically active wt CTRC and 8 SGPI-2 variants, we also determined the K  I  values with an independent, residual enzyme activity-based assay using synthetic substrate (Figure S6) and found that the two methods provide very similar K  I  and K  D  values, which validated the data obtained by the FP approach (Table 1). Therefore, all subsequent calculations are based on data obtained by the FP measurements.
Monitoring proteolytic degradation of SGPI-2 variants with HPLC and MS

SGPI-2 variants I6, I9, and I13 (15 muM) were incubated with wt CTRC enzyme (150 nM) at 25 C in 100 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM CaCl2 pH 8.0 buffer. Aliquots were withdrawn at 3, 6, 27, 52, 75, 116, 139, and 192 h, and the proteolytic reactions were immediately stopped with 5% formic acid (final concentration). All samples were stored at -20 C. Right before the Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS) measurements, all samples were incubated for 30 min at 60 C with 5 mM TCEP (final concentration) to reduce disulfide bonds.

Mass spectrometric experiments were performed on a high-resolution hybrid quadrupole-time-of-flight mass spectrometer (Waters Select Series Cyclic IMS, Waters Corp., Wilmslow, UK). Leucine enkephalin was used as Lock Mass standard. Chromatographic separations were performed on a Waters Acquity I-Class UPLC system, coupled directly to the mass spectrometer, using a Waters Acquity BEH C4 column (2.1 x 150 mm, 2.1 mum). Linear gradient elution (0 min 5% B, 1 min 5% B, 8 min 50% B) with eluent A (0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in water, V/V) and eluent B (0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in acetonitrile V/V) was used at a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min at 60 C. High-resolution mass spectra were acquired in the 350-2000 m/z range in positive ion mode. UV detection was performed at 220 and 280 nm (Table S2).
In silico modeling and analysis of the selected SGPI-2 clones

All model structures were generated with AlphaFold version 2.3.1 (Jumper et al. ) from the SGPI-2 amino acid sequence EVTCEPGTTFKDKCNTCRCGSDGKSAXCXXXXCXQ, where the different P4-P4' (XCXXXXCX) loop sequences used are listed in Table 2 and Table S3. The use of structural templates from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) option was enabled. The databases were downloaded on February 1, 2023. All model structures have undergone the built-in relaxation step of AlphaFold. For each sequence, the best ranking model with the highest per-residue model confidence (pLDDT) score was analyzed (Jumper et al. ). Per model mean pLDDT scores provided by AlphaFold are shown in Table S3. Protein Preparation Wizard (Madhavi Sastry et al. ) from Schrodinger Suite 2022-3 package (Schrodinger Release 2022-3: Schrodinger, LLC, New York, NY, 2022) was used to create bonds (CONECT lines in the structure files) to proximal sulfurs in all models. Hydrogen-bonds in the models were counted with UCSF ChimeraX version 1.5 (Pettersen et al. ) using its precise criteria for hydrogen bonding (Mills and Dean ). The enzyme binding loop of the inhibitor was defined as positions 27-34 (P4-P4') of the SGPI-2. From the ensemble of all inhibitor models, the backbone structure of the binding loops was extracted and aligned. From the binding loop structures which originally had P2 Thr, the loop which was least different from the mean of these structures were chosen as the representative (medoid) structure. All loop structures were then superimposed on this medoid. Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) from this medoid were calculated for each binding loop structures. RMSD and dihedral angle calculations on the models were done by the ProDy application programming interface version 2.4.0 (Zhang et al. ).

Evolutionary conservation profiling of SGPI-2

We compared the amino acid sequences of natural SGPI-2 homologs in order to reveal positional residue-conservations due to natural evolution. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
A novel directed protein-evolution-based strategy to identify key inhibitor residues that prevent productive proteolytic digestion

Canonical loop residues of reversible inhibitors that occupy the substrate binding groove of the target proteinase can fulfill two types of functions: contribute to binding affinity and/or prevent productive proteolytic digestion. We argued that the two functions can be dissected by using a point-mutant pair of target serine proteases, one being wild type (wt), while the other is an inactive variant, in which the catalytic serine is replaced by an alanine (S195A), but the other substrate binding groove residues and therefore the geometry of the substrate binding site remain unchanged (Krishnan et al. ; Pineda et al. ). We produced a library of the investigated canonical protease inhibitor such that all canonical loop positions carrying non-Cys residues are fully randomized and displayed the library on the surface of M13 phage. Then, we selected the inhibitor-phage library for binding separately on a wt serine proteinase and its S195A point mutant.

The logic of our comparative directed protein evolution procedure is illustrated in Figure 2.

Comparative directed inhibitor-evolution to identify proteolysis-preventing loop residues. The SGPI-2 library explained in Figure 1 is displayed on M13 phage and selected independently on wt CTRC and catalytically inactive S195A CTRC. Binding-selected individual SGPI-2 variant phage clones were tested for stable binding both to their original (either wt or S195A) target as well as the other target using an ELISA that detects bound M13 phage. We defined four classes of clones by comparing their wt CTRC/BSA and S195A CTRC/BSA ELISA signal ratios. We assigned a clone to the inhibitor-type class if its wt CTRC/BSA ratio was >=3 and its S195A CTRC/BSA ELISA signal ratio was >1; that is, it is a specific binder that might bind weaker to the mutant enzyme than to the wt. We defined substrate-type clones by an S195A CTRC/BSA ELISA signal ratio >=3 paired with a wt CTRC/BSA signal ratio close to 1. Substrate-type phage clones are presumed to suffer proteolysis in the reactive loop or elsewhere. Variants having S195A CTRC/BSA ELISA signal ratio >=3 while wt CTRC/BSA signal ratio in the 1-3 range were defined as intermediate-types. Clones having <3 target/BSA ratio on both enzyme forms were considered non-specific BSA/plastic-binders.

We displayed the SGPI-2 library illustrated in Figure 1 on the surface of M13 phage and selected the library members for binding to wt CTRC or catalytically inactive S195A CTRC in independent experiments. Then, we tested the phage-displayed, binding-selected individual SGPI-2 variants for stable binding both on their original wt or S195A target as well as on the other target, that is, wt for S195A-selected and S195A for wt-selected variants, using an ELISA detecting surface-bound M13 phage. For each clone, the ELISA signals on wt or S195A CTRC were compared to an ELISA signal on target-free control well blocked by BSA. We considered the binding effective when the target/BSA ELISA-signal ratio equals or exceeds three.

We defined three functional variant types based on the ELISA tests. Effective binders of wt CTRC were considered inhibitor-type variants as these clones were not productively hydrolyzed during the 2 h incubation time of the ELISA. All such clones were effective binders of the S195A CTRC as well. Effective binders of the S195A CTRC, which, on the other hand, had a wt CTRC / BSA signal ratio about one, that is, did not stably bind wt CTRC, were presumably productively hydrolyzed by the active enzyme and were considered substrate-type variants. This broad category encompassed phages that were likely cleaved in the reactive loop of the displayed SGPI-2, but also clones that may have been proteolyzed elsewhere within the SGPI-2 molecule or the phage surface. We also defined an intermediate-type group of variants that are effective binders of the S195A CTRC but have a wt CTRC / BSA signal ratio within the 1-3 range. Variants that do not effectively bind any of the two targets are non-specific BSA/plastic binders.
Binding selections on catalytically active versus inactive CTRC identifies inhibitor-type and substrate-type SGPI-2 variants

The same SGPI-2 phage library we previously published (Szabo et al. ) was freshly made and contained 5 x 108 variants. On wt CTRC selection, a 200-fold enrichment was reached in the 2nd selection cycle; therefore, no further rounds were performed. On S195A CTRC, we reached a 10-fold enrichment in the 3rd panning cycle, which did not improve in the 4th round. Individual clones from the 2nd wt CTRC selection cycle and from the 3rd and 4th S195A CTRC selection cycles were tested for original target and cross-target binding with phage-ELISA (Figure 2). As the 4th round provided mostly sibling clones that are identical at the DNA level, we narrowed our testing to the 3rd round clones. The emergence of siblings can be a sign of enhanced display-level of the given clone on M13 phage or enhanced propagation of the clone by the bacteria, or a serious drop of sub-library diversity due to "over-selection." All clones producing a higher than 3-fold ELISA signal compared to the BSA control on any of the two targets were sequenced at the DNA level.
Based on the ELISA signals, 95% of the ELISA-positive clones could be assigned either as substrate-type or as inhibitor-type variant (Tables 3 and 4).

From the wt CTRC selection we identified 40 clones that were unique at the DNA level (Figure 3a). Out of these, 37 are effective binders of both targets and were classified as inhibitors, two clones fell into the intermediate-type category, and only a single clone was substrate-type. From the S195A CTRC selection we identified 33 unique sequences (Figure 3b). The phage-ELISA tests split this group essentially in two; 15 clones (45.5%) were assigned as inhibitor-type (Figure 3e) while 16 clones (48.5%) as substrate-type, prone to proteolysis in the reactive loop or elsewhere. The remaining two clones were intermediate-type (6%). The logo representing all 52 inhibitor-type clones (37 from wt and 15 from S195A CTRC selection) is shown in Figure 3c. Comparison of the logos demonstrates that, in addition to the binding-selection, the activity of wt CTRC puts significant extra selective pressure on the canonical inhibitor, as only variants corresponding to a well-defined sequence pattern can stably bind to the active enzyme (Figure 3a).

Notably, the inactive S195A CTRC selected both inhibitor-type (45.5%) (Figure 3e) and substrate-type (48.5%) variants that are characteristically different, the inhibitor-type group having a well-defined sequence pattern similar albeit not identical to the one generated by wt CTRC selection, while the substrate-type lacks a discernible pattern. Many of these clones had reactive-loop sequences that contained no chymotrypsin-sensitive P1 residues or contained extra Cys residues suggestive of misfolding. Presumably, when incubated with active CTRC, these phage clones would suffer proteolysis outside of the reactive loop. It is interesting that even without the extra selection pressure, about half of the clones have a capacity for proteolysis resistance and these have some common characteristic features. Not surprisingly, the combined pattern of the S195A CTRC-selected clones (Figure 3b) represents a diluted version of the S195A CTRC-selected inhibitor-type pattern. As mentioned, the S195A CTRC-selected binding loop sequence pattern of the inhibitor-type subgroup (Figure 3e) differs to some extent from the one selected by wt CTRC (Figure 3a), which will be discussed in the next section.

The sequence pattern of the randomized (i.e., the two non-randomized Cys omitted) positions characteristic of the inhibitor-type clones (Figure 3c) (Y/A),T,(L/F/M),(M/L),L,(D/E) is broadly similar to the pattern that we determined from a previous selection against wt CTRC (Szabo et al. Figure 1b) (A/G/Y),T,(M/L),(M/L),L,(D/E) (Szabo et al. ).

The sequence patterns of the inhibitor-type and the substrate-type groups are clearly distinct. Out of the 52 inhibitor-type clones, 46 (88.5%) have consensus amino acid residues at least at four randomized positions (Tables 3 and 4), while the remaining 5 (9.6%) and 1 (1.9%) carry three and two consensus amino acid residues, respectively. Within the substrate-type group, the number of such positions is typically less than three. The only clone having three consensus residue types (indicated as underlined) is 2.2.08/I8 with the WWLLLV randomized sequence.
Sequence characteristics of inhibitor-type versus substrate-type clones

Out of the 73 clones tested by phage-ELISA, we identified 37 inhibitor-type clones selected on wt CTRC and 15 inhibitor-type clones selected on S195A CTRC. As both sets were defined by a capacity to stably bind to wt CTRC in the phage ELISA tests, it is not surprising that their sequence patterns are rather similar (Figure 3a,e). This shows that no inhibitor-type clones with novel inhibitory loop patterns were evolved on the inactive protease. We note that while the members of the set containing 37 wt CTRC-selected inhibitor-type clones, hereafter referred to as the 37-set, had to withstand productive cleavage in the 3-h selection time, members of the set containing 15 S195A CTRC-selected inhibitor-type clones, hereafter referred to as the 15-set, were not challenged that way, allowing for some room for difference in the selected clones. In fact, although the size of the 15-set is not large enough to draw statistically significant statements, we observed some trend-like sequence pattern differences between the two sets as follows.

At the P4 position, wt CTRC preferred a Tyr and, at lower degree, a Trp, while S195A CTRC did not select any aromatic residues at this position and preferred aliphatic side chains. At the P1-P1'-P2' segment, a common Leu-Met-Leu sequence motif was characteristic for both sets, but while at the P1 position, wt CTRC accepted Phe, Met, and Tyr in addition to the dominant Leu, S195A CTRC selected only Leu.

The overall most conserved position in the combined 52-set of inhibitor-type clones is P2, as 41 clones carried a Thr at this position (Figure 3c). It is notable, however, that 9 variants out of the 37-set and 2 variants out of the 15-set, that is, altogether 11 variants carried alternative Asp/Ser/Tyr/Leu/Gly P2 residues. Interestingly, however, in the small subset of the non-Thr P2 variants, each member was highly enriched in consensus residues at the other five randomized positions (Tables 3 and 4) suggesting that only a large number of optimal residues at other positions can compensate for the lack of a Thr P2. Most notably, none of the substrate-type variants had a Thr at their P2 further corroborating the inhibitory role of P2 Thr. It suggests that a lack of a P2 Thr enhances the substrate-type nature of the peptide (Table 4). Altogether, these observations highlight the unique importance of a P2 Thr in resisting productive proteolysis.
In P4', both enzymes selected for inhibitors with acidic residues (Asp and Glu) that can form salt bridges with a basic cluster on the CTRC, but variants with Trp and Tyr were also overrepresented.
Binding affinities of recombinant SGPI-2 variants determined on wt and S195A CTRC help interpreting the results obtained by directed evolution

Directed protein evolution delivered an information-rich dataset on the difference of inhibitor-type and substrate-type clones, providing testable hypotheses. For the direct tests, we designed a set of 13 SGPI-2 variants (listed in Table 1) that were produced as recombinant proteins, and their affinity to wt CTRC and S195A CTRC was determined. The first six SGPI-2 variants I1-6 were designed to study the P4 and P1-preferences of wt and S195A CTRC. Variants I7-11 were designed to test the side-chain-dependent functional importance of P2. From a different aspect, I8-9 and I12-13 were incorporated to represent substrate-type and intermediate-type clones, respectively, while the I1-6, I10, and I11 variants represented the inhibitor-type group.

Twelve out of the thirteen variants were successfully produced in large enough quantities for isolating them in homogeneous form. Only SGPI-2 variant I8 (clone 2.2.08) having the exceptionally hydrophobic canonical loop sequence of WCWLLLCV, could not be isolated as it was gradually lost during the purification steps. This represents a case when a hydrophobic protein is not stable in solution as a free recombinant protein but can be expressed and kept in a functional form on the surface of M13.
The other 12 SGPI-2 variants were successfully purified to homogeneity as verified by HPLC and mass spectrometry (MS).
We determined the binding affinities of the 12 SGPI-2 variants to wt and S195A CTRC with a competitive fluorescence polarization (FP) titration method as described in section 2.
Binding affinities on wt versus S195A CTRC dissect inhibitors and substrates and highlight specific roles of the catalytic Ser of the protease and the P2 Thr of the inhibitor

Each of the 12 SGPI-2 variants was incubated with wt CTRC for 24 h, after which the residual enzyme activity was measured. For 2 out of the 12 variants, the enzyme activity was the same as in the inhibitor-free CTRC control, indicating that these 2 variants were completely inactivated by progressive hydrolysis (Table 1). The other 10 variants stably suppressed CTRC activity, that is, were found to be inhibitors. Out of the two intermediate-type clones (based on ELISA-tests), 2.3.01 (I12) turned out to be an inhibitor, while 2.3.02 (I13) turned out to be a substrate (Table 1).

Interestingly, in FP measurements using FITC labeled SGPI-2 I1 as a tracer, which is a potent CTRC inhibitor that lowered the effective enzyme concentration in the sample, we could determine K  D  values for all SGPI-2 variants, including the 2 substrate ones, both on the inactive S195A CTRC as well as on the active wt CTRC (Table 1). While the 10 functional inhibitors all bound to wt CTRC stronger than to the S195A mutant, in the case of the 2 substrates, the opposite was observed. This trend, which was already recognized from the phage-ELISA results (Tables 3 and 4, 5th column), is visualized in the form of calculated   G values (Figure 4).

Different binding preference of inhibitors and substrates towards wt CTRC and S195A CTRC. Dissociation constant (K  D ) based binding energy ( G) values were calculated from the  G = RT ln K  D  equation for each enzyme-inhibitor pair. The different binding preference of a given SGPI-2 variant towards the wt and S195A CTRC enzymes was determined from the difference between the two binding-energy (  G) values. Negative values that are exclusive for inhibitor variants (dark gray) indicate more stable complexes with wt CTRC, while the positive values of the substrate variants (light gray) indicate more stable complexes with S195A CTRC.

The Ser195Ala mutation in the CTRC eliminates a potential H-bond between the enzyme and the SGPI-2 variant. Therefore, variants that can halt the catalytic machinery of the active enzyme, that is, the inhibitors form more stable complexes with wt CTRC than with S195A CTRC. In contrast, the substrate variants become progressively hydrolyzed by wt CTRC while staying intact in the S195A complex, and that is why these variants form more stable complexes with S195A CTRC in spite of the missing H-bond contact.

The mean   G value of the 10 inhibitors is -2.81 +- 1.37 kJ/mol (Table 1 and Figure 4), which represent a relatively narrow range. If we focus on the 8 inhibitors having P2 Thr, the mean absolute value of   G increases, while the scattering decreases: -3.3 +- 1.0 kJ/mol. Compared to that, the two non-Thr P2 inhibitors have significantly smaller absolute   G values, -1.2 kJ/mol (P2 Ser) and -0.5 kJ/mol (P2 Trp). It strongly suggests that the geometry of the substrate-binding groove of wt CTRC and S195A CTRC are essentially identical when they are not liganded, and it also implies that when the P2 is a Thr, it organizes the inhibitory loop into the same conformation in that groove in the wt and the S195A CTRC enzyme. Therefore, the   G values reflect mainly the presence or absence of a certain interaction that can be formed only through Ser195. It also suggests that the presumed P4' and P1 preference of the two CTRC forms are not significantly different. When, however, the inhibitor carries a non-Thr/Ser P2 residue, the conformation of the inhibitory loop is different. As we will show, three-dimensional structural models are congruent with this interpretation.
Testing proteolytic hydrolysis of the substrate-type variants with LC-MS

To test whether SGPI-2 variants I9 and I13 are indeed substrates, we incubated them with wt CTRC and with Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS) we proved that I9 and I13 were fully digested within 2 days, and both variants were at first cleaved at the P1-P1' site (Table S2). At identical conditions, the P1-P1' cleaved form of the functional inhibitor I6 was present only in 3%. The three enzyme-free controls showed no SGPI-2 degradation.
In silico structural analysis of the evolved SGPI-2 variants

As already mentioned, based on their relative binding efficacies to wt and S195A CTRC in ELISA tests, phage-displayed SGPI-2 variants were assigned either to the inhibitor-type or to the substrate-type subset, and only a minority was assigned to the intermediate-type subset. A major finding was that all variants having a P2 Thr belonged to the inhibitor-type subset, that is, not even a single clone behaved in a substrate-like manner, which identified P2 Thr as a key residue that prevents productive cleavage of the displayed variant. Note that P2 Thr is a wild-type residue in SGPI-2, and it is highly conserved by natural evolution in the Pacifastin family of canonical inhibitors.

There were 10 clones having a P2 Ser, which similarly to Thr has a beta-carbon hydroxyl, but unlike Thr, lacks the methyl group. Out of these, six clones (1.1.29, 1.1.30, 1.1.31, 1.1.32, 2.1.14, and 2.3.01) were assigned to the inhibitor-type and four clones (1.2.01, 2.2.01, 2.2.02, and 2.2.03) to the substrate-type set. One of the inhibitor-type clones (2.3.01) was first assigned as intermediate-type, but later proved to be an inhibitor (I12 in Table 1). The wt CTRC selected four inhibitor-type and one substrate-type P2 Ser clones, while S195A CTRC selected two inhibitor-type and three substrate-type P2 Ser variants.

The above observations implied that: (i) at P2, even the least perturbing replacement of the wild type Thr with a Ser can lead to loss of inhibitory function; (ii) there should be an underlying mechanism that explains the superiority of P2 Thr versus Ser; and further mechanisms should also exist that render some P2 Ser variants inhibitor-type while others substrate-type. We decided to study these questions as follows.

We noticed that in the inhibitory-type subset, all clones containing a non-Thr, for example, Ser residue at P2 matched the consensus pattern (Y/A),T,(L/F/M),(M/L),L,(D/E) at most, if not all, the other evolved (non-P2) positions, while deviation from the consensus pattern rendered these non-Thr P2 clones substrate-type. We wondered what kind of characteristic structural features are dictated by the different sequence patterns and how these could determine the observed functional differences of the inhibitor-type versus substrate-type groups. Ideally, this should be revealed by high-resolution methods such as NMR for the free inhibitor or X-ray crystallography for the free inhibitor and/or the inhibitor-enzyme complexes. Due to the large number of inhibitor variants, this approach would have been rather demanding. Therefore, we decided to test whether AlphaFold 2-based model structures show any distinctive features in terms of conformation or hydrogen bond network (HBN) that might separate the inhibitor-type and substrate-type variants.

We modeled the structure and HBN of all clones with AlphaFold 2.3.1, generating five models for each variant, and selected the one having the highest mean pLDDT score for further analysis. This model-level confidence was always at least 84% for the selected structures (Table S3).
Inhibitor-type and substrate-type variants differ in the structure of their evolved loop

First, we analyzed the structure of the evolved P4-P4' loop of 47 P2 Thr-containing SGPI-2 variants and identified the clone having the lowest RMSD from the mean of these 47 structures. This was then chosen to represent the structure of the given set, and we refer to it as the medoid structure. Then, for all variants, that is, the 57 inhibitor-types, 19 substrate-types and two intermediate-types we determined the RMSD values compared to the medoid and summarized the results as a bar diagram (Figure 5 and Table S3).

P4-P4' loop RMSD values of SGPI-2 variant structures compared to the medoid structure. Dark gray bars indicate inhibitor-type, light gray bars intermediate-type and white bars substrates-type variants. The order of SGPI-2 variants corresponds to the 7th column of Table 2. In the inlet we represent the average values of RMSD +- SD (A) of the three functional groups compared to the medoid structure. The one-letter symbols for amino acids above the bars indicate the type of the P2 residue in the corresponding SGPI-2 variant.

To quantify the differences between the inhibitor-type and the substrate-type subsets, we calculated the mean RMSD values for both groups. The data show that even though the calculated structures correspond to free, un-complexed SGPI-2 variants, the loop structure of the inhibitor-type set is rather uniform as from the medoid loop structure it has a small 0.175 +- 0.157 A mean RMSD value. On the other hand, the substrate-type set has significantly higher 0.642 +- 0.339 A mean RMSD value indicating a different and potentially more diverse group. The RMSD of the intermediate-type variants is similar to that of the inhibitor-type structures.

Compared to the inhibitor-type variants, the substrate-type variants on average have a 3.5-fold higher RMSD value. Although the standard deviation is also higher in the substrate-type group, even the structures with the lowest RMSD values are clearly well above the average of the inhibitor-type subset. Nevertheless, even in the case of the substrate-type group, these RMSD values are small compared to the 1.1-1.6 A accuracy of AlphaFold (Jumper et al. ; Terwilliger et al. ).

Most inhibitor-type variants had low RMSD values, but among them, there are some variants with significantly higher than group average RMSD values. In order to locate the outlier structures, and reveal the local conformational differences, we plotted the Phi and Psi torsion angles for each residue within the P4-P4' loop of the inhibitor-type variants (Figure 6).

Structural models of the inhibitory loop conformation of all inhibitor-type variants and the corresponding Phi and Psi torsion angles. The modeled P4-P4' loop structures of the non-Ser/Thr variants on panel (a) are visualized from two different views by superimposing the backbone structures of the loops. The medoid of the P2 Thr variants is highlighted with a thicker light blue line. The colors indicate the identity of the P2 residue (inbox). The gray arrow indicates the scissile P1-P1' peptide bond. To quantitate the conformational differences at each position, Phi and Psi backbone torsion angles were determined for each loop residue of each inhibitor-type SGPI-2 variant. Phi and Psi values that are connected correspond to the same variant. The identity of the P2 residue is indicated with different colors (inbox). The X-axis represents SGPI-2 sequence numbering (27-34) corresponding to the P4-P4' segment. On the panel-pair (b) all SGPI-2 variants are included, while on panel-pair (c) the P2 Thr variants are replaced by their single medoid conformation for a clearer view on the conformation of the non-Thr variants.

The medoid structure is based on the P2 Thr-carrying clones that are all inhibitor-types. When we analyzed the data, we observed that the 47 P2 Thr and 4 P2 Ser containing inhibitor-type clones have almost identical loop geometry, which is especially characteristic at the level of Phi values at the 28-30 and Psi values at the 27-31 segments. In contrast, the six non-Thr/Ser P2 inhibitor-type variants show a different loop geometry that did not specify a single distinct structural group. P2 Gly and Asp variants (clones 2.1.15 ACGLLLCY and 1.1.33 YCDLLLCD) just slightly diverged from the highly conserved P2 Thr/Ser loop, while the P2 Tyr and Trp variants (1.1.35 GCYLMLCD and I7 ACWLMLCD) showed a distinct loop geometry. For the two P2 Leu variants (1.1.37 ACLLLLCD and 1.1.36 ACLLLLCE) AlphaFold predicted structures that regarding to their Psi values, were noticeably different from those of the medoid within the 28-30 segment.

Interestingly, the P2 Ser SGPI-2 variant set falls into two different structure types, and it correlates to their inhibitor versus substrate-type classification (Figure 7). Compared to the substrate-type set, the inhibitor-type set has lower RMSD from the medoid structure (Figure 5) and their loop structures are similar to those of the P2 Thr variants. While the loop geometries of the substrate-type variants differ from those of the inhibitor-type set. Note that individual substrate-type variants differ significantly not only from the inhibitor-type variants but also from each other.

Characteristic structural differences between the inhibitor-type and the substrate-type P2 Ser SGPI-2 variants. The AlphaFold modeled structures of a representative inhibitor-type (clone 2.3.01/variant I12) and substrate-type (clone 2.2.02) P2 Ser variant are on panel (a, b), respectively (coloring scheme is the same as on Figure 1). Note that the inhibitor-type variant possesses, while the substrate-type variant lacks the central loop-stabilizing hydrogen bond between the P2 Ser and Asn15 sidechains. Panel (c) illustrates that the conformation of the P4-P4' loop of the substrate-type P2 Ser variants (blue) differs from that of the inhibitor-type P2 Ser medoid (thicker orange). Gray arrow indicates the scissile bond between the P1 and P1' residues. Panel (d) quantifies the observed conformational difference in terms of Phi/Psi values. Phi and Psi values belonging to the same variant are connected. Orange lines and blue lines indicate inhibitor-type and substrate-type variants, respectively. The X-axis represents SGPI-2 sequence numbering (27-34) corresponding to the P4-P4' segment.
Inhibitor-type and substrate-type variants differ in their intramolecular hydrogen bond networks

We determined the number of intramolecular hydrogen bonds at three levels: (i) the entire SGPI-2 structure, (ii) within the P4-P4' loop, and (iii) separately for the P2 residue (Table 2). Analysis of the hydrogen bonds that connect the P2 into the HBN, identifies a particularly interesting hydrogen bond between P2 (Xaa29) and Asn15, as it is present in almost all inhibitor-type clones, but does not occur in any of the substrate-like variants (Table 2). Group averages were determined for total, loop and P2 hydrogen bond contacts. On average, the number of hydrogen bonds in the inhibitor-type variants exceeds that of the substrate-types with 3.4, and from this difference, 2.7 maps to the P4-P4' loop. Out of this 2.7 loop-related difference, 1.4 maps to loop residue P2, again highlighting the central structural role of this residue. There are a few inhibitor-type variants where the P2 is involved only in a single hydrogen bond. These variants also have diminished numbers of loop- and total hydrogen bonds to a degree approaching those of the substrate-type clones (Table 2 highlighted with bold).

Importantly, the abovementioned structural analysis and this hydrogen bond network analysis identified the very same SGPI-2 variants as outliers from the otherwise homogenous set of inhibitor-type variants. These six inhibitor-type variants that have a non-Thr, non-Ser P2 all have reduced number of hydrogen bonds in all three categories, all of them make only a single H-bond through their P2 residue, and all of them lack the Xaa29-Asn15 hydrogen bond (where Xaa29 is the P2 residue). Note that this Xaa29-Asn15 contact is missing from all variants of the substrate-type set.

In our AlphaFold 2.3.1-based modeling study, both the Phi-Psi torsion angle-based and the intramolecular HBN analyses dissected the set of the P2 Ser-containing variants in the very same subsets that were constructed based on inhibitor type versus substrate type behavior in the phage-ELISA test. Therefore, in our hands, AlphaFold 2.3.1 highly reliably predicted the structural effects of mutations. Based on the literature, some studies support (McBride et al. ) while others question (Laurents ; Pak et al. ) this capacity of the software. All of our results indicate that it is the loss of the hydrogen bonding contacts around the P2 Ser, and particularly the loss of the P2 Ser-Asn15 hydrogen bond, that mostly differentiates the substrate-type subgroup from the inhibitor-type subgroup. While the structural features brought up by AlphaFold modeling require experimental structural verification by NMR or X-ray crystallography to be fully accepted, we find it remarkable that in the case of the substrate-type group, AlphaFold did not generate those types of structures that it congruently predicted for the inhibitor-type set.

This was not the case with the six non-Thr/Ser inhibitor-type variants where the same modeling based structural analysis did not distinguish inhibitor-type variants from substrate-type structures. In a scatter plot presenting the number of total and loop hydrogen bonds versus the RMSD of the P4-P4' loop from the medoid (Figure 8) the two categories for P2 Thr/Ser variants separate nicely but the six P2 non-Thr/Ser variants intermingle with the substrate-type variants.

Scatter plot visualization of the combined results of the hydrogen bond network and the RMSD analysis of the SGPI-2 variant structures. The x-axis indicates the RMSD values determined for each individual SGPI-2 P4-P4' loop compared to the medoid. The y-axis shows (a) the total number of hydrogen bonds (b) the number of hydrogen bonds in the loop for a given variant. Inhibitor-types are green, substrate-types are purple and intermediate-types are yellow. The shape of the sign indicates the type of the P2 amino acid residue; Thr/Ser are indicated with diamond, while circles correspond to any other residue than Thr/Ser.

Only experimental structural studies could tell whether this may indicate some limitations of the modeling procedure, or this is due to genuine alternative loop stabilization solutions that do not rely on the P2. In this subgroup, representing 10% of the observed inhibitor-types, we found no pre-stabilized P4-P4' loops in SGPI-2 and the P2 position was unhooked from the intramolecular HBN. Quite remarkably, however, in this small, six-member group, on average 4.7 +- 0.5 out of the five randomized non-P2 loop-positions harbored phage-display-selected consensus amino acid residues. We argue that the large number of optimal residues at the non-P2 loop positions provide enough binding energy to properly stabilize the P'-side new N-terminus in the acyl-enzyme without the typical intramolecular HBN found for the P2 Thr/Ser inhibitor-type variants. In the substrate-type group both the pre-stabilizing HBN and the consensus loop sequence for favorable ligand-enzyme contacts are absent, hence they cannot position their P'-side N-terminus in the acyl-enzyme such that it halts complete hydrolysis by the protease (Nemeth et al. ).

Finally, with the online tool ConSurf, we analyzed how natural evolution conserved amino acid residues at each position in SGPI-2 homologs. The results (Figure 9) are in complete agreement with our experimental findings from directed protein evolution and our results from in silico structural modeling. At amino acid residue 29, which corresponds to the P2 position, almost exclusively Thr, and to a minor extent Ser, were selected by natural evolution, while at position 15, Asn was strongly conserved. Notably, besides the fold-stabilizing six Cys residues, the two most conserved positions are 15 and 29. We also note that amino acid 31, corresponding to the P1' position, harbors residues with fully or partly aliphatic sidechains.

Sequence logo visualizing positional residue conservation of natural SGPI-2 homologs. The input sequence set was generated by a multiple sequence alignment of natural SGPI-2 homologs via a ConSurf search. The color-coding is the same as in Figure 3. The X-axis represents SGPI-2 sequence numbering, where 27-34 corresponds to the P4-P4' segment. The logo was created with the WebLogo application (https://weblogo.berkeley.edu/logo.cgi).
CONCLUSIONS

The purpose of the present study was to identify amino acid residues in the binding loop of a canonical protease inhibitor that are critical for preventing productive hydrolysis while allowing for or contributing to high-affinity binding. We employed a directed evolution approach where we presented the substrate-binding site of the active protease and its inactive mutant to a canonical serine protease inhibitor in which the binding loop amino acid residues were randomized. The substrate-binding grooves of the catalytically active and inactive enzymes should recognize the same, presumably rather diverse set of binders. However, while all members of this set would form stable complexes with the inactive enzyme, only those that avoid productive hydrolysis are expected to form stable complexes with the active enzyme. By measuring the binding capacities of the two selected populations, we could dissect the selected variants into two major sets, inhibitor-type and substrate-type. We tested this new approach by using human CTRC (active and Ser195Ala inactive mutant) as the protease targets and SGPI-2 as the canonical serine protease inhibitor.

In agreement with our prediction, we found that active CTRC selected only inhibitor-type clones, whereas Ser195Ala CTRC selected approximately equal number of inhibitor-type and substrate-type clones. We purified a set of SGPI-2 variants as recombinant proteins and conducted fluorescence-polarization (FP), enzyme-inhibition, and proteolytic stability tests that verified the inhibitor- or substrate-like nature of the SGPI-2 variants. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the Ser195Ala mutation did not change the specificity of the substrate-binding groove of CTRC but decreased the binding energy by about 3 kJ/mol.

The combined results of the selected sequence patterns, phage-ELISA, FP, enzyme-inhibition assays, and proteolytic stability tests identified the P2 Thr residue as the critical determinant of binding loop stability against proteolytic degradation. At this position, Thr and to a smaller extent the physicochemically similar Ser was predominantly selected, with rare occurrences of Asp, Tyr, Leu, and Gly. Besides P2, position P1' also plays a role in resistance against proteolysis. Here, residues with long hydrophobic sidechains such as Leu and Met were selected.

Exceeding our expectations, AlphaFold-based modeling revealed some specific features that separated the structures of the SGPI-2 variants almost perfectly into the same inhibitor-type and substrate-type subsets that had been defined based on functional assays. These subset-specific structural features also mapped to the P2 position, to an intramolecular hydrogen bond formed between the P2 Thr or Ser hydroxyl with Asn15, which is located underneath the inhibitory loop. This intramolecular hydrogen bond turned out to be an organizing center of a more extended loop-stabilizing hydrogen-bond network that provides the inhibitor-type variants with a rather uniform and stable loop conformation.

When this hydrogen-bond network forms, and the P1 residue fills the deep apolar S1 binding pocket, the P1' Leu/Met stably occupies the S1' pocket. Additional inhibitor-type features are the conserved P4 Tyr/Ala and P4' Asp/Glu that can stabilize the two extremities of the binding loop in the substrate-binding groove. These features together enable a loop conformation that can readily bind to the substrate-binding groove without any significant conformational change, and position the P1 carbonyl group to the catalytic Ser195 in such a manner that even when an acyl-enzyme is formed, the Leu or Met side chains would block the access of the water molecule that could otherwise hydrolyze the scissile bond.

We found that inhibitor-type variants that have non-Thr/Ser P2 residue contained optimal residues at the P4, P1', and P4' positions, which provided rare but functional alternative solutions. In contrast, the substrate-type variants that lack the P2 Thr/Ser-organized hydrogen-bond network and/or the ideal combination of P4/P1'/P4' residues, form an acyl-enzyme complex with active CTRC, in which the scissile bond is accessible for water molecules.

In summary, our novel directed protein-evolution-based approach was able to identify loop-residues on a reversible serine proteinase inhibitor that impart resistance to productive hydrolysis of the scissile bond. We found that these residues are also among the most conserved ones in natural SGPI-2 homologs. The observed and modeled functional and structural roles of these residues are congruent with the "clogged-gutter" mechanism previously proposed for an evolutionarily and structurally unrelated inhibitor family (Radisky and Koshland ). Our findings suggest that the "clogged-gutter" mechanism might be universal within the 18 families of reversible serine proteinase inhibitors and that our approach may be generally applicable to provide a straightforward solution for identifying the hydrolysis-preventing residues in all the remaining such families. This information can support better understanding of the structure-function relationships and natural evolution of protease inhibitors and facilitate rational design of novel inhibitor folds.

passages.text: Untapped potential: exploring clinical pharmacists as antibiotic stewardship ambassadors
Objective:
To describe inpatient clinical pharmacists' interventions on injectable antibiotics and assess their impact on prospective audit and feedback (PAF) by the antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP).
Design:
Retrospective cohort study.
Setting:
Freestanding, quaternary-care, pediatric and obstetric hospital.
Methods:

We identified all clinical pharmacist interventions (iVents) documented on injectable antibiotics from November 1, 2020, through October 31, 2022. PAF performed on injectable antibiotics during the same timeframe was captured. We reported characteristics of clinical pharmacist iVents on injectable antibiotics. We also compared the incidence of PAF recommendations (PAFR) between PAF cases with prior iVent documentation for the same patient and antibiotic and those without preceding iVent documentation.
Results:

A total of 5,277 iVents were documented on injectable antibiotic orders. Cefazolin had the highest volume of iVents (13%). Antibiotic dose optimization was the most frequent iVent type (34%). A total of 5,152 PAF were documented by ASP pharmacists on injectable antibiotics during the study period, with 1,782 (34%) resulting in a PAFR. A total of 999 PAF (19%) had a prior iVent; 4,153 PAF did not. Comparing the two groups, the incidence of a PAFR was significantly higher in the PAF with prior iVent group compared to the PAF without prior iVent group (383/999, 38% vs 1,399/ 4,153, 34%; P = 0.006). Antibiotic discontinuation was the most common type of PAFR in both groups.
Conclusions:

Clinical pharmacists serve as ASP ambassadors, intervening on injectable antibiotic orders to improve prescribing. Future efforts to expand and incorporate clinical pharmacists in ASP initiatives are warranted.
Introduction

Pharmacists' expertise is recognized as an essential element of antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs).   While much of the attention has focused on infectious diseases (ID)-trained pharmacists, all clinical pharmacists, regardless of their clinical setting or title, are capable of contributing to stewardship initiatives.

Prospective audit and feedback (PAF) - the retrospective evaluation of prescribed antibiotics - is recognized as a core ASP strategy by the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America.   While the method and procedures for performing PAF may vary by institution and range from formal handshake rounds to tele-stewardship, the overarching goal remains the optimization of antibiotic prescriptions.   Additional benefits include reductions in antibiotic resistance and the incidence of Clostridioides difficile infection.

There are limited data on the types of interventions identified by clinical pharmacists at hospitals with an ASP. The primary objective of this study was to characterize the types of interventions (iVents) made by clinical pharmacists on injectable antibiotic orders in a pediatric hospital setting. Additionally, we sought to determine whether the incidence of ASP PAF recommendations (PAFR) differed based on the presence of a preceding clinical pharmacist iVent.
Methods
Study setting

Lucile Packard Children's Hospital Stanford is a university-affiliated, 413-bed hospital that delivers quaternary-level pediatric and obstetric care. Our pharmacy practice model consists of clinical pharmacists responsible for order verification, medication preparation, or participation in family-centered rounds, based on their training and expertise. All inpatient antibiotic orders are evaluated by a clinical pharmacist for appropriateness during order review and verification. During this review, pharmacists may identify interventions to improve antibiotic prescribing. Interventions identified during order verification or rounding are documented as iVents attached to the medication order in the electronic health record (EHR) (Epic Systems Corporation Verona, Wisconsin). Content documented within an iVent includes the intervention type and subtype (Supplemental Table 1).

Our ASP team includes two physicians trained in pediatric ID and two full-time clinical pharmacy specialists who are board-certified in ID by the American College of Clinical Pharmacy.   Our ASP pharmacists perform PAF every weekday, which includes a review of all inpatient orders for injectable antibiotics that have been active for at least 48 hours.   All PAFs performed, regardless of whether a recommendation is identified or not, are documented in the EHR through a customized smart form. Recommendations identified during PAF are communicated to the primary team through their rounding clinical pharmacist or directly to the team if no clinical pharmacist is present. This strategy allows for a collaborative practice and bidirectional education between the clinical and ASP pharmacists.
Study design

This was a single-center retrospective review of interventions documented as iVents by clinical pharmacists on inpatient orders for injectable antibiotics from November 1, 2020, through October 31, 2022. All iVents documented on an injectable antibiotic order were included, as long as the iVent type was unique. PAF and PAFR on injectable antibiotics during this timeframe were also captured. iVents and PAF were excluded if data was missing from the documentation record. Given that obstetric services are excluded from the PAF program, iVents documented on obstetric antibiotic orders were excluded. Data captured from the iVent report included patient identifiers, antibiotic name, intervention date and time, intervention type and subtype, and, if available, intervention outcome. PAF data included patient identifiers, antibiotic name, audit date and time, and, if applicable, recommendation type and recommendation acceptance. This project was reviewed by Stanford University's institutional review board and determined to be local quality improvement work that did not meet the definition of human subjects' research.
Study analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to characterize iVents. We matched PAF and iVents based on patient identifiers, antibiotic name, and time between the PAF and iVent. A PAF was classified as linked to an iVent (ie, PAF with prior iVent group) if they were documented for the same patient and the same antibiotic and the PAF was documented within 4 days following the iVent. A 4-day window was selected to capture iVents documented during weekends or holidays with subsequent PAF on the next business day. Due to the difference in documentation terminology for iVents and PAFR, interventions and recommendations were translated to a recoded recommendation type based on similar intent to enable comparisons (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2). Comparison of the proportion of PAFR between the PAF with prior iVent group and PAF without prior iVent group was performed using the chi2 test in SPSS (2021 IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 28.0. Armonk, New York: IBM Corp) with alpha set at 0.05.

Results

During the study period, there were 29,753 inpatient orders for an injectable antibiotic, excluding orders from the obstetric units. A total of 6,325 iVents were documented on antibiotic orders. Application of our inclusion/exclusion criteria resulted in a cohort of 5,277 unique iVents on injectable antibiotics for analysis (Figure 1). Less than half of iVents included outcome documentation (2,324/5,277, 44%) with 1,731 (74%) iVents documented as accepted, 29 (1%) as rejected, and 564 (24%) documented as informational or non-applicable. The majority of iVents were documented on antibiotic orders from an acute care unit (Table 1). Cefazolin had the highest volume of iVents (716, 13%). The most frequent type of iVent was antibiotic dose optimization (1,811, 34%; Table 2).
Flowchart of iVent screening.

A total of 5,152 PAF were documented by ASP pharmacists on injectable antibiotics during the study period, resulting in 1,782 (35%) PAFR. Vancomycin had the highest volume of PAFR (244/1,782, 14%) and the most common PAFR type was to discontinue the antibiotic (445/1,782, 25%; Table 2 and Supplemental Table ). A total of 999 PAF (19%) had a preceding iVent documented for the same patient and antibiotic; the remaining 4,153 PAF did not have a prior iVent identified. Comparing the two groups, the PAF with prior iVent group had a significantly higher proportion of PAFR than the PAF without prior iVent group (383/999, 38% vs 1,399/ 4,153, 34%, P = 0.006; Table 3). Antibiotic discontinuation was the most common type of PAFR, regardless of prior iVent, accounting for 24% (91/383) of recommendations in the PAF with prior iVent group and 25% (354/1,399) in the PAF without prior iVent group (Table 3). Dose optimization was also similar between groups (16% [63/383] of PAF had a PAFR in the PAF with prior iVent group vs 14% [192/1,399] in the PAF without prior iVent group).

Discussion

We report the first pediatric study describing the types of antibiotic stewardship interventions identified by clinical pharmacists and their impact on subsequent ASP PAFR. Our study demonstrated that clinical pharmacists perform many antibiotic interventions as ASP ambassadors, with most interventions focused on antibiotic dose optimization. Such interventions may improve patient safety by ensuring that patients are receiving the appropriate antibiotic dose based on their indication, their renal function, and their clinical status. Our findings align with previous studies that identified dose adjustment as one of the most frequent pharmacist interventions on antibiotic orders for adult patients, accounting for approximately two-thirds of interventions.

We discovered that the types of interventions by clinical pharmacists differed from ASP pharmacist PAFR. The most common clinical pharmacist interventions were dose optimization, order clarification, and drug administration. Our ASP pharmacists' most common recommendations were antibiotic discontinuation, therapy modification, and duration of therapy suggestions. There may be multiple reasons why the types of interventions differ between clinical and ASP pharmacists. A critical determinant of clinical intervention is the available clinical data, including microbiologic information. The difference in available information at the time of order verification vs ASP review may impact the scope and depth of pharmacist interventions. For example, at the time of antibiotic order entry, a clinical pharmacist could recommend dose optimization, and subsequently an ASP pharmacist performing PAF 48-72 hours later could recommend discontinuing the therapy based on negative culture data.

The difference in intervention types made by clinical and ASP pharmacists may also be attributable to limitations in clinical pharmacist training in ID and antibiotic stewardship, which has been recognized as an important factor in prior studies.   Clinical pharmacist exposure to and training in ID is highly variable, particularly for those without post-graduate training or certification.

Creation, collaboration, and maintenance of institutional guidelines, protocols, and policies related to antibiotics are often the responsibility of an ASP pharmacist which requires familiarity with the most recent ID literature. This may not be the same for clinical pharmacists focused on other areas of practice. Investment in education for front-line clinical pharmacists through tuition assistance programs for ASP/ID-specific continuing education courses can help enrich the ID/ASP educational experience for clinical pharmacists. Likewise, providing institutional resources (eg, institutional guidelines for empiric antibiotic selection) could not only help with an institutional shift to more evidence-based practice, but strengthen antibiotic interventions made by clinical pharmacists.

While we observed a higher incidence of PAFR when PAF followed a clinical pharmacist's iVent compared to when it did not, the clinical significance of the small absolute difference is uncertain. It is possible that the presence of an iVent is a marker of antibiotic order complexity increasing the likelihood of a subsequent intervention by the ASP. For example, when a provider selects an antibiotic from a condition-specific, EHR-embedded order set, pharmacist-led dose optimization may be needed less often.   Additionally, the order is more likely to be appropriate for the selected condition, reducing the chances of an ASP pharmacist PAFR. The frequency of PAFR types was consistent whether or not there was a prior iVent, supporting the idea that intervention targets and opportunities differ between clinical and ASP pharmacists.

Our single-center experience might not fully mirror practices at other institutions. Given our study's dependence on documentation of interventions as iVents by clinical pharmacists, it is important to note that documentation may be absent and not reflective of all interventions clinical pharmacists are identifying and communicating. Due to the strict matching procedure requiring that PAF and iVent interventions be performed on the same antibiotic, if an iVent led to a change in antibiotic, the new antibiotic would be categorized as a PAF without a prior iVent. As a result, we may have underestimated the impact of clinical pharmacists' iVents on preventing future PAFR. Of note, the iVent type to change or discontinue the patient's antibiotic was uncommon.

Our study highlights the contributions of clinical pharmacists in optimizing antibiotic therapy. The observed differences in intervention types between ASP and clinical pharmacist cohorts may be attributable to the difference in timing and data availability upon antibiotic review. Given their contributions, clinical pharmacists are important ASP ambassadors. Continued investment in clinical pharmacist education and development will be essential to support ongoing antibiotic prescribing improvement efforts.

passages.text: Clinical efficacy and effect on neurotransmitter levels of Shaoma Zhijing granules in children with tic disorders
Objective
To investigate the clinical efficacy of Shaoma Zhijing Granules in treating pediatric tic disorders and its impact on plasma neurotransmitter levels.
Methods

Eighty pediatric patients with tic disorders were randomly divided into the Shaoma Zhijing group (40 cases) and the Tiapride group (40 cases). The Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (YGTSS) scores, clinical efficacy, and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) syndrome evaluations were compared at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks after treatment. Ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) was used to analyze the changes in plasma neurotransmitter levels before and after treatment.
Results

Compared with baseline, both groups showed a decrease in YGTSS scores and TCM syndrome scores at 4 weeks and 8 weeks after treatment (P < 0.05). No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups (P > 0.05). The effective rates were 90% for the Shaoma Zhijing group and 80% for the Tiapride group, with the incidence of adverse reactions being 2.5% and 15%, respectively. After 8 weeks, serum levels of glutamic acid (Glu), aspartic acid (Asp), dopamine (DA), norepinephrine (NE), and epinephrine (E) in both groups were significantly lower than baseline (P < 0.05), while gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels were significantly higher (P < 0.05). Significant differences were also observed between the two groups in DA, NE, E, and GABA levels after treatment (P < 0.05).
Conclusion

Shaoma Zhijing Granules demonstrate significant clinical efficacy and good safety in treating pediatric tic disorders. They effectively improve symptoms, thereby contributing to the enrichment of the TCM diagnostic and treatment system for pediatric tic disorders.
Introduction

Tic disorders (TD) are common neurodevelopmental disorders in children. Clinically, they are characterized by involuntary motor and/or vocal tics. In recent years, the incidence of pediatric tic disorders has been steadily increasing, with a reported annual incidence rate of approximately 6.1% in China. These disorders can significantly affect children's learning, social interactions, and personality development.

The pathogenesis of TD is not fully understood. Most researchers believe that its onset may involve genetic factors, brain structural abnormalities, and neurotransmitter imbalances due to brain dysfunction. Neurotransmitters, which primarily facilitate information transmission within the nervous system, have been extensively studied in children with TD. Current research focuses on biogenic amines [dopamine [DA], epinephrine [E], norepinephrine [NE]] and amino acids (glutamic acid [Glu], aspartic acid [Asp], gamma-aminobutyric acid [GABA], histidine [His], tryptophan [Trp]). Excessive DA activity or DA receptor hypersensitivity is a widely accepted mechanism underlying TD. Based on this theory, the 2020 Chinese Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pediatric Tic Disorders recommends tiapride, a classic DA receptor blocker, as a first-line treatment. Several studies have confirmed the efficacy of tiapride in treating pediatric TD. However, long-term use may cause side effects such as like dizziness, drowsiness, fatigue, and weight gain, and symptoms often relapse after discontinuation, which can reduce patient compliance. From a traditional medicine perspective, TD is often categorized in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) as "liver wind," "convulsions," or "chronic convulsions." Shaoma Zhijing Granules (SMZJG, also known as 5-ling granule, or TSupport/T92 under U.S. development), is an innovative TCM formulation, combines multiple herbs to calm liver yang, extinguish wind and stop spasms, clear fire and resolve phlegm, and enhancing efficacy while reducing toxicity. This study included 80 children with TD in a randomized controlled trial to compare the efficacy of Shaoma Zhijing granules and tiapride, as well as their effects on plasma neurotransmitter levels. Tiapride was included as a positive control due to its proven efficacy in treating TD.

passages.text: Materials and methods
Clinical data collection

Children with TD who visited the outpatient department of Wuxi Children's Hospital between November 2022 and October 2023 were selected for the study. A total of 80 participants were enrolled and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the experimental group (Shaoma Zhijing granule, 40 cases) or the control group (Tiapride, 40 cases) using a random number table. The detailed allocation process is presented in the flowchart (Figure 1). All participants received monotherapy without any concomitant medications. Importantly, outcome assessors were blinded to treatment allocation throughout the study. In the Shaoma Zhijing group, there were 26 boys and 14 girls, aged 5-14 years. Of these, 12 were 5-7 years old, 19 were 8-10 years old, and 9 were 11-14 years old, with an average age of 8.30 +- 1.70 years. The disease duration ranged from 6 months to 4 years, with an average of 17.70 +- 7.65 months. In the Tiapride group, there were 27 boys and 13 girls, aged 6-13 years. Of these, 10 were 5-7 years old, 19 were 8-10 years old, and 11 were 11-14 years old, with an average age of 8.85 +- 1.92 years. The duration of illness ranged from 6 months to 5 years, with an average of 17.23 +- 8.70 months. There were no statistically significant differences in gender, age, duration of illness comorbidities, difficulty falling asleep, or parental mental disorders between the two groups (P > 0.05), as shown in Table 1. All selected children underwent rigorous clinical symptom screening and were diagnosed by two neurologists and two TCM doctors. The diagnostic criteria referred to the "Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Tic Disorders in Children (2020 Edition)", the 5th edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders" (DSM-5), and the diagnostic standards from the "Clinical Practice Guidelines for Traditional Chinese Medicine Pediatrics: Tic Disorders". This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Wuxi Children's Hospital (Ethics No.: WXCH2022-09-079). All participants and their families signed informed consent forms.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Inclusion Criteria: (1) Meets the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for tic disorders, with frequent tic symptoms lasting for more than 6 months; (2) Meets the TCM diagnostic criteria for hyperactive liver wind syndrome. The diagnostic criteria are as follows: Primary symptoms: frowning, blinking, grimacing, mouth opening, shoulder shrugging, head shaking, arm swinging, leg kicking, loud shouting, frequent and intense tics, or vocal tics with obscene language. Secondary symptoms: irritability, hot palms and soles, restless sleep, dry stools, dark yellow urine, red tongue with a thin yellow or greasy yellow coating. To diagnose Hyperactive Liver Wind Syndrome with Phlegm-Fire internal disturbance, at least two primary symptoms and two secondary symptoms must be present, along with tongue and pulse diagnosis.
Explanation of TCM Terms:

Hyperactive Liver Wind Syndrome: In TCM, this syndrome refers to an overactivity of liver yang leading to internal wind, manifesting as involuntary movements and tics, often associated with irritability and restlessness.
Liver Wind: A TCM concept referring to internal wind movement caused by liver dysfunction, primarily manifested as tremors, tics, or other involuntary movements.
Phlegm-Fire: A condition characterized by the accumulation of phlegm and excessive heat in the body, resulting in symptoms like irritability, restless sleep, and a greasy yellow tongue coating.
(3) Aged between 5 and 18 years, regardless of gender; (4) Provides informed consent and can accept the prescribed treatment plan and follow-up requirements.

Exclusion Criteria: (1) Does not meet the inclusion criteria; (2) Clearly diagnosed with epilepsy, chorea, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), intellectual disability (ID), athetosis, Wilson's disease, or autoimmune diseases; (3) Children with severe diseases involving the heart, brain, liver, kidneys, or hematopoietic system; (4) Clinically significant abnormal electrocardiogram; (5) Known allergy to TCM or its components; (6) Other serious diseases.
Treatment methods

Shaoma Zhijing granules (Tasly Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd., National Medicine Standard Z20190022, specification: 2.5 g/bag) were taken orally. The main ingredients are Radix Paeoniae Alba (Bai Shao), Rhizoma Gastrodiae (Tian Ma), Fructus Tribuli (Ji Li), Ramulus Uncariae (Gou Teng), Ganoderma (Ling Zhi), Caulis Polygoni Multiflori (Shou Wu Teng), Semen Ziziphi Spinosae (Suan Zao Ren), vinegar-prepared Fructus Schisandrae (Wu Wei Zi), Fructus Gardeniae (Zhi Zi), Rhizoma Arisaematis cum bile (Dan Nan Xing), and Radix Scutellariae (Huang Qin). For children aged 5-12 years: 5 g per dose (2 bags), three times a day; For children aged 13-18 years: 7.5 g per dose (3 bags), three times a day. Tiapride (Jiangsu Enhua Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., specification: 100 mg/tablet) was administered at a dose of 50-100 mg per day, divided into 2-3 doses. After 1-2 weeks, the dose was gradually increased based on the patient's condition and age to 200-400 mg per day, with regular follow-up. The treatment and observation period for both groups was 8 weeks.
Observation indicators
Tic severity

The severity of tic symptoms in both groups of children was analyzed using the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (YGTSS) before treatment, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks after treatment. The YGTSS assessment was conducted by two experienced neurologists who received standardized training prior to the study. The evaluators were blinded to the participants' treatment assignments throughout the assessments to ensure objectivity and consistency. Main Indicators: Tic scores are composed of five elements: type, number, frequency, intensity, interference, and complexity of motor and vocal tics. Each element is scored from 0 to 5. The total score for motor tics and vocal tics is 25 points each. Secondary Indicators: The YGTSS also assesses the level of social impairment caused by tics. This refers to the distress caused by tics in areas such as self-esteem, family life, social interactions, and academic or work performance. The impairment is evaluated on a 6-point scale (none to severe), corresponding to scores from 0 to 50, with higher scores indicating greater social impairment.
TCM Syndrome Grading and Quantification Standards:
No symptoms: 0 points;
Mild symptoms, such as only frowning or blinking, or only opening mouth or grimacing: 1 point each;
Frequent occurrence: 2 points each;
Constant occurrence: 3 points each.
No symptoms: 0 points
Presence of symptom: 1 point each.

Primary Symptoms: The primary symptoms consist of five items: frowning and blinking, opening the mouth and grimacing, shaking the head and shrugging shoulders, flinging hands and kicking legs, and making strange noises or uttering foul language. Secondary Symptoms: The secondary symptoms include five items: irritability, hot palms and soles, restless sleep, dry stools, and dark yellow urine.
Efficacy evaluation

The clinical efficacy of the two groups of children was evaluated using the YGTSS before treatment, and 8 weeks after treatment. The clinical efficacy is categorized into four levels: (1) Cured: Symptoms and signs have basically disappeared within 8 weeks of medication, with a total score reduction of >=90%, and no recurrence for more than 1 month; (2) Significantly Effective: Tics have significantly reduced within 8 weeks of medication, with a total score reduction of >=70% but <90%. (3) Effective: Tics have somewhat improved within 8 weeks of medication, with a total score reduction of >=30% but <70%; (4)Ineffective: No improvement or worsening of tics within 8 weeks of medication, with a total score reduction of <30%;
The total effective rate is calculated as follows:
Total Effective Rate = (Number of cured cases + Number of significantly effective cases + Number of effective cases Total number of cases) x 100%
Plasma neurotransmitter level detection

All enrolled children were instructed to maintain consistent daily habits before sample collection, including following a light diet, avoiding major lifestyle changes, minimizing the intake of caffeinated stimulants (such as coffee, cola, etc.), and refraining from medications that could influence neurotransmitter levels. They were also advised to ensure adequate sleep before sample collection. Venous blood samples (3 ml) were collected in the early morning after fasting from both groups at initial enrollment and after 8 weeks of treatment. The samples were placed in heparin anticoagulant tubes and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes. After centrifugation, the plasma was stored in a freezer at -20 C. The levels of neurotransmitters [DA, GLU, GABA, Asp, NE, E, Trp, His, Tyrosine (Tyr)] in the plasma were analyzed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Quantitative analysis was conducted using isotope-labeled internal standards to ensure measurement accuracy and reliability. For each neurotransmitter, calibration curves were generated using certified reference standards at concentrations spanning the physiological range. Quality control measures included: (1) analysis of low-, medium-, and high-concentration QC samples for internal quality control (IQC), and (2) participation in External Quality Assessment (EQA) programs to assess both intra- and inter-laboratory variability.
Statistical analysis

Data analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0 statistical software. A t-test was used for the measurement data of the two groups, with the measurement data expressed as (x +- s). The chi-square (chi2) test was used for categorical data. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Comparison of YGTSS scores before and after treatment in the two groups

YGTSS scores decreased significantly in both groups during the treatment period (Shaoma group: F = 49.1, P < 0.05; Tiapride group: F = 30.32, P < 0.05). At baseline, no significant difference was found between the two groups (Shaoma: 32.65 +- 11.28 vs. Tiapride: 31.35 +- 10.96; t = 0.523, P = 0.603). After 4 weeks of treatment, scores in both groups were significantly lower than baseline (P < 0.05), with no significant intergroup difference (t = -0.155, P = 0.877). By week 8, scores had further declined (Shaoma: 12.23 +- 8.04; Tiapride: 13.48 +- 9.38), showing significant improvement compared to week 4 (P < 0.05), while intergroup differences remained statistically non-significant (t = -0.640, P = 0.524). (See Figure 2).
Comparison of YGTSS scores in two groups at different times (x +- s).
Comparison of TCM syndrome efficacy before and after treatment in the two groups

TCM syndrome scores demonstrated significant improvement in both groups over time (Shaoma group: F = 106.22, P < 0.05; Tiapride group: F = 89.33, P < 0.05). Baseline scores were comparable between groups (Shaoma: 11.33 +- 3.17 vs. Tiapride: 11.60 +- 3.54; t = -0.366, P = 0.716). By week 4, scores in both groups had decreased markedly from baseline (P < 0.05), with no significant difference between groups (t = 0.194, P = 0.847). At week 8, scores reached their lowest values (Shaoma: 3.45 +- 2.05; Tiapride: 3.63 +- 2.70), demonstrating significant improvement compared to week 4 (P < 0.05), while intergroup differences remained non-significant (t = -0.327, P = 0.745) (see Figure 3).
Comparison of TCM syndrome scores in two groups at different times (x +- s).
Comparison of clinical efficacy between the two groups

The efficacy rates in the Shaoma Zhijing Granule group for the 5-7, 8-10, and 11-14 age groups were 91.7%, 89.5%, and 88.9%, respectively, with an overall efficacy rate of 90%. In the Tiapride group, the efficacy rates for the same age groups were 80%, 78.9%, and 81.8%, with an overall efficacy rate of 80%. A statistically significant difference was observed in the overall efficacy rates between the two groups (P < 0.05) (see Table 2).

As demonstrated in Figures 4, 5, baseline neurotransmitter levels (Glu, Asp, DA, NE, E, GABA) were comparable between groups (all P > 0.05).
